k1p1-22.text: a supervised rule: driven by labels and errors

k1p2-26.text: an input that is 0 never changes its weight

k1p3-2.name: text#2
k1p3-2.text: Every update moves in the right direction

k1p3-6.name: text#6
k1p3-6.text: since $x_{i0}=1$, $\|\mathbf{x}_i\|^2\ge1$: $s$ always rises for error $+1$ and falls for $-1$

k1p3-20.text: e.g. wrong on $(0,1)$: $s$ goes from $-1$ to $1$, up by exactly $\|\mathbf{x}\|^2=2$

k1p4-2.text: By hand: learning OR from all zeros

k1p5-2.text: The line is pushed toward the wrong points

k1p6-2.name: text#2
k1p6-2.text: The final weights are the OR gate from KP01

k1p6-14.name: text#14
k1p6-14.text: The only difference: the weights were not worked out by a person

k1p6-15.text: given only data and right answers, it corrected itself

k1p7-2.text: When it stops, and when it never does

k1p7-12.name: text#12
k1p7-12.text:
stops after finitely many updates
(perceptron convergence theorem, not proved here)

k1p7-24.name: text#24
k1p7-24.text: stop when a whole pass makes no update

k1p8-2.name: text#2
k1p8-2.text: Fix only when wrong, but not fixed in one go

k1p8-7.name: text#7
k1p8-7.text: Myth: “each sample is fixed once and never wrong again”

k1p8-8.name: text#8
k1p8-8.text: Not so: in pass 1 the point $(0,0)$ was fixed, then broken by the update for $(0,1)$, and wrong again in pass 2. One update only moves this sample's $s$ the right way.

k1p8-10.name: text#10
k1p8-10.text: With labels 0 and 1 there are three error cases. If we use $+1$ and $-1$, can the rule be shorter and show its geometry?

steps.label: KP02 Change weights only when wrong
The feedback loop · 1/8
steps.speakerNotes: Every weight of the KP01 neuron had to be worked out by hand. In 1958 Rosenblatt added feedback.

steps.label: The feedback loop · 1/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: For each sample, compute the sum s and the output, then compare with the correct label.

steps.label: The feedback loop · 1/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Ask: was it right?

steps.label: The feedback loop · 1/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: If right, do nothing; only if wrong push the weights one step the right way, then take the next sample. This is a supervised rule.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/8
steps.speakerNotes: The update rule is a single line. The error y minus o can only be 0, plus 1 or minus 1.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Error 0: right, no change. Error plus 1: should have fired but did not, add eta times x, s rises.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Error minus 1: fired but should not have, subtract eta times x, s falls. An input that is 0 adds 0, so its weight stays.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Think of turning knobs: too quiet, turn up; too loud, turn down; right, leave it.

steps.label: Always the right direction · 3/8
steps.speakerNotes: After the update, this sample's sum becomes s plus eta times the error times the squared length of x. With x0 equal to 1, the squared length is at least 1.

steps.label: Always the right direction · 3/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A concrete case: weights 0, 0, minus 1 meet the sample 0, 1; s is minus 1, output 0, but the label is 1.

steps.label: Always the right direction · 3/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Adding the bias input, x is 0, 1, 1; the new weights are 0, 1, 0 and the new s is 1. The increase is exactly the squared length of x, which is 2.

steps.label: Always the right direction · 3/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: One update only guarantees that this sample's s moves the right way.

steps.label: Step-by-step trace · 4/8
steps.speakerNotes: The data come in the order 0 0, 0 1, 1 0, 1 1; start from all zeros with learning rate 1.

steps.label: Step-by-step trace · 4/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Pass 1: the point 0 0 is wrong, s is 0 and output 1 but the label is 0, so the bias drops by 1; then 0 1 is wrong, w2 gains 1 and the bias gains 1.

steps.label: Step-by-step trace · 4/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Pass 2: 0 0 is wrong again, broken by the update for 0 1; 1 0 is wrong. Pass 3: 0 0 is wrong once more.

steps.label: Step-by-step trace · 4/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Five updates in all, ending at weights 1, 1, minus 1. Pass 4 is all right with no updates, so it stops.

steps.label: Step-by-step trace · 4/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: 5 updates in all; pass 4 is all right → stop

steps.label: The moving line · 5/8
steps.speakerNotes: At the end of pass 1 the line is horizontal and the point 0 0 is still in the firing region; the red ring marks the error.

steps.label: The moving line · 5/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: At the end of pass 2 the line has turned diagonal but still passes through 0 0.

steps.label: The moving line · 5/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: At the end of pass 3 the line sits at x1 plus x2 equals 1 and all four points are right. Each update pushes the line toward a wrong point.

steps.label: The moving line · 5/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: end of pass 3: \mathbf{w}=(1,1,-1) all four points right solid: label 1 · open: label 0 · dashed: s=0

steps.label: Back to KP01 · 6/8
steps.speakerNotes: The OR gate worked out in KP01 has weights 1, 1, minus 1 and threshold 1.

steps.label: Back to KP01 · 6/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The weights learned here are also 1, 1, minus 1.

steps.label: Back to KP01 · 6/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Exactly the same. The difference is that this time a person did not work them out; the machine found them from data and answers alone.

steps.label: Back to KP01 · 6/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The only difference: the weights were not worked out by a person given only data and right answers, it corrected itself KP01's question is answered: let the weights learn themselves

steps.label: When it stops · 7/8
steps.speakerNotes: On linearly separable data the Perceptron always stops after finitely many updates. This is the perceptron convergence theorem, not proved here.

steps.label: When it stops · 7/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: On non-separable data it never stops. The XOR of KP04 is such a case.

steps.label: When it stops · 7/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In code it is a double loop and stops when a whole pass has no update. Also, starting from 0, learning rate 2 gives exactly twice the weights of rate 1, with identical predictions.

steps.label: When it stops · 7/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: starting from 0, \eta=2 just doubles the weights: same predictions stop when a whole pass makes no update

steps.label: Summary and myth · 8/8
steps.speakerNotes: The point of this unit: do nothing when right, push the weights one step the right way when wrong.

steps.label: Summary and myth · 8/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A common myth: that a sample, once fixed, is never wrong again. In fact the point fixed in pass 1 is broken by a later update.

steps.label: Summary and myth · 8/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A question for the next unit: with labels plus and minus 1, can the update rule be shorter?

steps.label: Summary and myth · 8/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With labels 0 and 1 there are three error cases. If we use +1 and -1, can the rule be shorter and show its geometry? next unit: ±1 labels shrink the rule to one line
